prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level
for conceiving the cubic-kilometre IceCube detector and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep the same configuration, but I hold the IceCube half with less confidence than the clock half. B043 is now the best-supported item in the room: it is in four configurations, is an alternative for three more members, and no one disputes its confirmation in Sr, Yb and Hg or the 10^-18 comparisons between independent laboratories. The two names map onto two identifiable contributions, Katori's magic-wavelength lattice and first strontium demonstration, and Ye's record accuracy and many-body clock physics. Kroll's reply to Mehlig answers the overlap worry for me: the 2005 comb prize solved counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems, and neither recognised a many-atom lattice free of Doppler and recoil shifts. The citation should name the demonstrated 10^-18 performance, not the pending redefinition of the second. B010 supplies the discovery element that the clock lacks. The diffuse TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrino flux is established by several independent analysis channels well above five standard deviations, which is the part of the case I would rest the prize on; the source associations are corroborating, not foundational. Halzen is the originator of the cubic-kilometre concept and of the scientific case for it, and that is the least contested individual role in the programme. Together the two parts are distinct achievements, neither adjacent to the 2025 circuit prize, and they keep the union at three people.
statement.case_against: The IceCube credit remains the weak point and the chair's own question is not fully answered by the record in front of us. I cannot identify an individual contribution that decisively separates Halzen from Karle, whose detector construction and analysis leadership were essential, or from Yoshida, and a one-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds, built on AMANDA and with Baikal and ANTARES as precursors, will look arbitrary to part of the community. The source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) are at roughly three to four and a half sigma, so they should not appear in the citation. A prize with one laureate on one half and two on the other is also unusual. On the clock side, Mehlig's question is fair: the physics gain so far is better tests of constants and relativity, with no deviation from existing theory seen, and the claim rests on an instrument-enabled change in what can be measured. If the committee judges that no clean IceCube credit exists, the better course is B043 alone, which is the cleanest single configuration on the list, and I would accept that over adding Karle and Yoshida and breaching the cap.

responses.point: Olsson ranks IceCube low because a collaboration of hundreds makes any three-name credit fragile, and asks whether the source evidence is as robust as the diffuse flux. She keeps magic-angle graphene first on the strength of a prediction and an experiment that each have a clear leader.
responses.response: The source evidence is not as robust as the diffuse flux and I would not put it in the citation: the diffuse flux is established above five sigma in independent channels, while TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane are in the range of three to four and a half sigma. That is why my citation names the detector and the discovery of the flux only. I accept her attribution point and have narrowed the credit to one name for that reason, but I disagree that graphene has the cleaner credit: Cao and Fatemi, Dean's group and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory leave it as contested as IceCube, and eight years without a settled pairing mechanism is a real maturity gap against two decades of neutrino detector development. I still keep B029 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson asks me directly what the decisive individual contribution to the IceCube discovery is, and says he would not rank B010 above circuit QED until that has a firm answer. He keeps B023 first and B043 as his first alternative.
responses.response: The honest answer is that Halzen's decisive contribution is conceptual and organisational, not a single measurement: he proposed scaling the AMANDA approach to a cubic kilometre, and made the case for the physics that justified building it. Karle's detector and analysis leadership is not separable in any clean way from that, and I cannot claim otherwise. I therefore treat B010 as the part I could drop. On circuit QED I read the 2025 prize as a timing problem, whatever its formal distinction from light-matter coupling, and the four-name credit forces an omission of Blais or Girvin that you yourself call the weakest part. Your own willingness to accept B043 as the consensus outcome if B023 fails on attribution is the most useful signal for me in this round.

responses.point: Danielsson shares my two-part configuration, prefers Halzen alone to a trio he admits is hard to defend, and would drop the IceCube half rather than invent an artificial trio. His reservation about B033 is attribution.
responses.response: We agree on the structure and on the fallback. I would add that the choice is not symmetrical: dropping the IceCube half leaves the clean B043 prize, whereas adding Karle and Yoshida breaks the three-person cap and would force out a clock laureate. On gamma-ray burst afterglows I still ranked it highly, and I do not see an attribution that handles van Paradijs, Piro, Djorgovski, Metzger and Frail within three names, so it does not enter my configuration even though we both regard it as mature.

responses.point: Kroll is troubled by IceCube attribution, cannot see a three-name subset the collaboration would accept, and ranks the clock alone as the cleanest and most mature prize, resisting a broader credit that would blur the distinction from 2005.
responses.response: His objection to a three-name IceCube subset is the strongest argument against my second part and I do not have a decisive reply beyond Halzen's role as originator. I accept his point that the clock is a sufficient prize by itself on the physics. My reason for pairing it is not that B043 lacks merit but that, as a measurement-science award, the committee may want a discovery alongside it. I would give that up if the committee cannot resolve the IceCube credit. I agree with him against widening the clock credit to comb-era names.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what physics a clock prize teaches that the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not, and notes that no deviation from existing theory has been seen. He ranks topological insulators first, with the Z2 classification as a new principle.
responses.response: What it teaches is that an ensemble of neutral atoms can be interrogated without Doppler or recoil shifts at a level where the clock resolves centimetre-scale gravitational redshifts and tests constants to new precision. That is demonstrated, not promised, though I concede it is a gain in what can be measured and not a new phenomenon. For B008 I accept his answer to the 2016 objection that time-reversal-invariant topological insulators were not recognised then, and I keep it as my second alternative. I still prefer Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, anchored in the quantum spin Hall effect, to any version that adds Hasan and the contested three-dimensional priority.

responses.point: Lindroth argues the prize should reward demonstrated performance and independent agreement between clocks, and that the citation should present the many-body and relativity results as physics, not only metrology.
responses.response: I agree, and I have kept the citation to the demonstrated 10^-18 performance. I accept her caution that agreement among atomic physicists is not independent evidence, so my own weighting rests on the cross-laboratory clock comparisons, which are independent. I do not insist on adding the many-body clock results to the citation, because they would invite the question of which names cover them.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept a one-name IceCube credit; if not, I would prefer B043 alone to a trio that breaches the cap.
Whether the supplied material resolves how Halzen's contribution can be separated from Karle's and Yoshida's, which I cannot settle from it.
Whether the committee regards B043 as a discovery within the intent of the prize or as measurement science needing a partner part.
Whether the maturity of magic-angle graphene will change within a few years in a way that makes it the preferred single achievement next time.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents work on PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, so astroparticle and gamma-ray instrumentation, including B010 and B033, is close to my own field and I hold a position on B010 in my configuration. No personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Halzen or any other named candidate is apparent from my profile, and I see no recusal requirement.
